An Early and Middle Bronze Age village on a terrace between two streams in the Troodos foothills, at the exact seam between the grain land of the Mesaoria and the copper-bearing pillow lavas. Steven Falconer and Patricia Fall have dug it since 2004, and twenty-five radiocarbon dates put its six occupation phases between about 2050 and 1850 BCE. It is the clearest picture available of ordinary households that mined and smelted their own copper.

The largest stone plank figure excavated on Cyprus, recovered not from a tomb but from an open public space in the middle of the village, which is why it matters: it puts these figures into communal life rather than the grave.

en: A small industrial hamlet west of Ambelikou village, in the northern Troodos foothills beside Skouriotissa, one of the richest orebodies on the island. In 1942 modern miners broke into an ancient shaft and found pottery of about 2000 BCE in it, which brought Porphyrios Dikaios to the spot. Ambelikou remains the earliest place on Cyprus where copper mining itself, rather than the copper, can be proved, and it also produced a potter's workshop abandoned mid-job.

en: The largest Bronze Age burial ground known on Cyprus, spread over about six hectares of hard limestone crust on the south side of the Ovgos valley. It is also the most comprehensively robbed. When David Frankel and Jennifer Webb surveyed it in 2003 and 2004 they mapped 1,286 pillaged tombs, and argued that even a cemetery this badly damaged still carries readable information about population and wealth, and should not be written off to the bulldozer.

The survey's central figure, and the reason so many unprovenanced Cypriot Bronze Age pots in world collections are labelled simply 'Deneia'. Tomb architecture and the sherds left behind still gave a curve of rising population and rising funerary spending through the Bronze Age.

en: A north-coast cemetery of tombs cut into soft gypsum, dug by James Stewart in 1955. Its material is unlike anything at other Philia-phase sites and includes weapons that were made outside Cyprus, which is why the site sits at the centre of the argument about whether the Philia horizon means Anatolian migrants or only Anatolian fashions. Stewart thought the Philia style survived at Vasilia long after it had ended elsewhere, a view still contested.
Nine metal objects hidden beneath the plaster lining of a tomb passage, one of the largest metal groups of its date on the island and evidently placed there deliberately rather than dropped.

en: Not a village but an industrial quarter, now hemmed in by the villas of modern Pyrgos, excavated from 1998 by Maria Rosaria Belgiorno for Italy's National Research Council. Copper smelting, olive pressing, weaving, wine and perfumed oil were all carried on in one complex, with the olive oil apparently doubling as furnace fuel. An earthquake flattened it around 1850 BCE and thereby preserved the equipment where it stood.

en: A cluster of fortified sites on the plateau above the meeting of the Alykos and Yialias rivers in the middle of the Mesaoria, built and given up inside about a century and a half around 1750 to 1600 BCE. Barsak, on the cliff edge, had a double circuit wall with a ditch outside it; Nikolidhes, two kilometres to the south-west, was ringed by a wall some 900 metres long with a rectangular tower. Einar Gjerstad dug at Glyka Vrysi in 1924, Hector Catling surveyed the group in the 1950s, and Despina Pilides has excavated here in recent years. Whether these works were raised against raiders from the sea or against each other is the central unresolved question of the period.

en: A square fortress of cyclopean masonry on a hill above the south coast of the Karpass, with towers at three corners and flanking the gate and a cistern in its courtyard. The Swedish Cyprus Expedition dug it in 1929 and published it in 1935; tombs nearby date to about 1725 to 1600 BCE. It belongs to a group of forts thrown up as Cyprus turned from a society of villages into one with copper worth defending. The usual reading is that they guarded the routes from the mines to the coast, but whether they watched the sea, the roads or each other is still argued.
Walls of huge unworked blocks on a square plan, with corner towers and a gate passage flanked by two more, a design without Cypriot precedent and with Levantine and Anatolian relatives.

en: A mound of collapsed mudbrick on the west side of the Ovgos river, on what was then the shore of Morphou bay. Emily Vermeule dug it for Harvard and the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston, with Florence Wolsky, in 1971 to 1973; the events of 1974 ended the work and the team left the island for good. Under the mound lay a potters' quarter with kilns and clay-working floors, and rich rock-cut tombs whose Cretan, Egyptian and Levantine imports have made the site one of the fixed points for tying the Cypriot Bronze Age sequence to the Aegean one.

en: A Late Bronze Age town in the lower Maroni valley about 500 metres from the sea, with a coastal twin at Maroni-Tsaroukkas and an open anchorage offshore; taken together the localities cover something like 35 hectares. The British Museum opened tombs here in 1897, Gerald Cadogan excavated the settlement for the University of Cincinnati between 1982 and 1989, and Sturt Manning worked on the coastal site and its seabed in the 1990s. Its centre was an ashlar building given over to pressing and storing olive oil on a scale far beyond any household's needs, abandoned around 1200 BCE and then reoccupied as a sanctuary in the Iron Age.

A tripartite building roughly 30.5 by 21 metres, built partly of large finely cut and closely fitted blocks, with pressing installations and storerooms for olive oil. It is one of a small group of monumental buildings, with Kalavasos and Alassa, that mark the appearance of something like regional administration on Cyprus.

en: Two localities on a triangular plateau in the Troodos foothills, unknown to archaeology until a salvage survey in 1983 ahead of the Kouris dam. Sophocles Hadjisavvas dug them from 1984 to 2000 and published the final report in 2017. Paliotaverna, on the upper plateau, held a group of three monumental ashlar buildings, the largest a great pi-shaped complex; Pano Mandilaris, 250 metres to the south-east, was a crowded residential quarter with metalworking going on among the houses. Petrographic work on the clay of the Alashiya letters points to this stretch of the south coast rather than to Enkomi, which makes Alassa one of the candidates for where the king of Alashiya actually sat.

en: A miners' village on the north-western flank of the Troodos, in the Solea copper district beside Skouriotissa and Mavrovouni. It came to light in 1938 when the Cyprus Mines Corporation began to open the Apliki orebody, and Joan du Plat Taylor was asked to dig it in haste in 1938 and 1939. Lead isotope analysis has since matched almost every oxhide ingot yet tested, on Cyprus and abroad, to ores of this district and above all to Apliki, which makes this small and short-lived settlement the source of the metal the Bronze Age world was buying. Most of it has been eaten by modern open-cast mining; Taylor's notebooks were finally published in full in 2012.
